Case ID: Patan Jamal Vali v. State of Andhra Pradesh; Crl. Appeal No. 452 of 2021 (arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 1795 of 2021)
Court / Bench: Supreme Court of India; Dr D.Y. Chandrachud J (author), M.R. Shah J
Case type: Criminal appeal by special leave against conviction
Original court: High Court of Andhra Pradesh, Division Bench (judgment 03-08-2019); trial by Special Judge for SC/ST (PoA) Act cases-cum-VI Addl. District & Sessions Judge (judgment 19-02-2013)
Accused caste category: Not stated (charge under SC/ST Act s.3(2)(v) presupposes accused is not SC/ST)
Accused domicile/state: Resided in Gajulapalli village, Andhra Pradesh
Accused socioeconomic status: Pleaded at sentencing that he is a poor person earning his livelihood through coolie work
Victim socioeconomic status: Not stated for victim; trial court described victim's mother as an illiterate village woman
Accused–victim relationship: Acquaintance: worked with victim's brothers for two years and regularly visited the family home
Offence severity: IPC s.376(1) as it then stood: minimum 7 years, up to life; SC/ST Act s.3(2)(v): life imprisonment and fine
Physical harm: Contusion on left cheek; vaginal laceration with bleeding requiring sutures
Number of offences: Convicted on 2 counts at trial; 1 upheld finally
Premeditation/planning: Not expressly found; the Court noted the accused asked where the brothers were and entered the house in the family's absence
Motive: Not identified; Court held no evidence that the offence was committed on the ground of the victim's caste
Evidence type: Victim testimony (voice identification); eyewitnesses to the aftermath and apprehension; medical evidence; seized clothing
Key evidence accepted: Consistent testimony of PW1 (mother) and PW2 (victim), corroborated by PW3, PW4, PW5; medical evidence of PW10; accused apprehended at the spot
Confession/admission: In s.313 CrPC statement, admitted he used to visit the house to call the victim's brothers for coolie work
Witness credibility: Accepted. Defence argued in HC that a blind victim could not identify the accused; Court held a disabled witness's testimony is entitled to equal weight
Aggravating circumstances: Victim blind since birth; accused exploited familiarity with the family and their absence; intersecting vulnerability (gender, caste, disability)
Mitigating circumstances: Accused's poverty pleaded at trial; not accepted
Post-offence conduct: Tried to escape; caught at the spot and handed to police
Legal representation: Counsel for appellant in SC: Mr Harinder Mohan Singh (whether private or legal aid not stated)
Procedural irregularity: Trial court and HC failed to apply the 'on the ground' ingredient of SC/ST Act s.3(2)(v)
Appeal history: Sessions: convicted on both counts, life imprisonment each (concurrent). HC: affirmed. SC: s.3(2)(v) conviction set aside; s.376(1) conviction and life sentence upheld
Prosecution argument: Not separately recorded in SC judgment (State's case: accused raped victim in her house)
Defence argument: Offence under s.3(2)(v) not established, so a life sentence under s.376(1) was not in accordance with law
Legal principle applied: Pre-2016 s.3(2)(v) requires the offence to be committed 'on the ground' that the victim is SC/ST; mere knowledge insufficient for pre-amendment offences; intersectionality; equal weight to testimony of disabled witnesses
Precedent relied upon: Dinesh v. State of Rajasthan (2006) 3 SCC 771; Ramdas v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 2 SCC 170; Ashrafi v. State of UP (2018) 1 SCC 742; Khuman Singh v. State of MP (2019); Ravji v. State of Rajasthan (1996) 2 SCC 175; State of Karnataka v. Krishnappa (2000) 4 SCC 75; State of Punjab v. Prem Sagar (2008) 7 SCC 550
Sentencing rationale: Gravity of offence; victim blind since birth; accused aged 27, known to the family, exploited their absence; victim's SC status not extraneous to sentencing under s.376
Judicial aggravating factors: Victim's disability; accused's familiarity with the family; victim's intersecting vulnerabilities
Conviction outcome: Conviction modified (s.376(1) upheld; s.3(2)(v) set aside)
Other sentence/order: SC issued systemic guidelines on sexual violence against women with disabilities (judicial and police training, interpreters, disaggregated NCRB data)

Case ID: Satbir Singh & Anr. v. State of Haryana; Crl. Appeal Nos. 1735-1736 of 2010
Court / Bench: Supreme Court of India; N.V. Ramana CJI (author), Aniruddha Bose J
Case type: Criminal appeals by special leave against conviction
Original court: High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh (judgment 06-11-2008, Crl. Appeals 3-SB & 16-SB of 1998); trial court judgment 11-12-1997
Accused domicile/state: Not stated (prosecution by State of Haryana)
Offence category: Dowry death (abetment of suicide also charged)
Statute: IPC; Indian Evidence Act 1872 (presumptions); Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 (definition of dowry)
Offence severity: s.304B: minimum 7 years, up to life imprisonment; s.306: up to 10 years and fine
Number of offences: Convicted on 2 counts at trial; 1 upheld finally
Motive: Dowry: harassment over insufficient dowry, including a specific demand for a scooter
Evidence type: Testimony of deceased's father and brothers; medical evidence; statutory presumption (Evidence Act s.113B)
Key evidence accepted: Brothers (PW7, PW10) and father (PW6) on dowry harassment, including a disclosure about one week before death; doctor (PW3) found kerosene smell and 85% burns
Witness credibility: Found reliable, consistent and corroborative by trial court and HC; SC agreed
Aggravating circumstances: Death about one year after marriage; continued harassment for dowry soon before death
Procedural irregularity: None found in this case; SC flagged trial courts' casual recording of s.313 CrPC statements as a general concern
Appeal history: Trial: convicted under s.304B (7 yrs RI) and s.306 (5 yrs RI). HC: appeals dismissed. SC: s.304B upheld; s.306 set aside
Prosecution argument: Suspicious death within about a year of marriage; witnesses consistently described specific dowry demands
Defence argument: Accidental fire not ruled out; no dowry demand proved; demand not proximate to death
Legal principle applied: Ingredients of s.304B; 'soon before' means a proximate and live link, not 'immediately before'; s.113B presumption is mandatory once ingredients are proved; s.306 requires proof of suicide first
Precedent relied upon: Major Singh v. State of Punjab (2015) 5 SCC 201; Kans Raj v. State of Punjab (2000) 5 SCC 207; Rajinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2015) 6 SCC 477; Bansi Lal v. State of Haryana (2011) 11 SCC 359; Wazir Chand v. State of Haryana (1989) 1 SCC 244; Maya Devi v. State of Haryana (2015) 17 SCC 405; Shanti v. State of Haryana (1991) 1 SCC 371
Sentencing rationale: No separate sentencing discussion; s.304B sentence (7 yrs RI, the statutory minimum) left undisturbed
Conviction outcome: Conviction modified (s.304B upheld; s.306 set aside)
Other sentence/order: SC issued trial guidelines for s.304B cases (s.313 questioning, defence-evidence stage, caution about implicating distant relatives)

Case ID: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar & Anr.; Crl. Appeal No. 1277 of 2014 (@ SLP (Crl.) No. 9127 of 2013)
Court / Bench: Supreme Court of India; Chandramauli Kr. Prasad J (author), Pinaki Chandra Ghose J
Case type: Criminal appeal by special leave against refusal of anticipatory bail
Original court: High Court (Bihar) and Sessions Judge, both refusing anticipatory bail; dates not stated
Number of accused: 1 appellant (wife's allegations also name his parents)
Accused domicile/state: Not stated (case against State of Bihar)
Accused role: Principal accused (husband); in-laws alleged to have made dowry demands
Statutory provision: IPC s.498A; Dowry Prohibition Act s.4
Offence severity: s.498A: up to 3 years and fine; DP Act s.4: up to 2 years and fine (as stated in judgment)
Financial/property loss: Alleged demand of Rs 8 lakh, a car, an air-conditioner, a television etc.
Post-offence conduct: Alleged: wife driven out of the matrimonial home for non-fulfilment of dowry demand
Custody duration: Not stated (not in custody; provisional bail granted 31-10-2013)
Bail history: Anticipatory bail rejected by Sessions Judge, then by High Court; SC granted provisional bail 31-10-2013, made absolute 02-07-2014
Trial duration: Marriage 01-07-2007; FIR date not stated; still pre-trial at SC judgment
Procedural irregularity: Court identified a systemic pattern of routine arrests without s.41 CrPC satisfaction and casual magisterial authorisation of detention; no specific defect found in this case
Appeal history: Sessions: anticipatory bail refused. HC: refused. SC: appeal allowed
Legal principle applied: Arrest for offences punishable up to 7 years requires police satisfaction of necessity under s.41(1)(b)(ii) CrPC; s.41A notice of appearance; magistrate must scrutinise reasons before authorising detention (Art. 22(2), s.57, s.167 CrPC)
Precedent relied upon: No case precedents cited; relied on Law Commission Reports (152nd, 154th, 177th) and NCRB 'Crime in India 2012' statistics
Other sentence/order: Provisional bail made absolute; 8 directions to State Governments, police and magistrates on arrest and detention, applying to all offences punishable up to 7 years

Case ID: Shajan Skaria v. State of Kerala & Anr.; Crl. Appeal No. 2622 of 2024 (arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 8081 of 2023); 2024 INSC 625
Court / Bench: Supreme Court of India; J.B. Pardiwala J (author), Manoj Misra J
Case type: Criminal appeal by special leave against refusal of anticipatory bail
Original court: High Court of Kerala (Crl. Appeal No. 906 of 2023, judgment 30-06-2023), affirming Special Judge, SC/ST (PoA) Act, Ernakulam Division (order 16-06-2023)
Accused caste category: Not SC (stated: appellant is not a member of a Scheduled Caste)
Accused religion: Not established. The complainant's complaint, reproduced in the judgment, alleges the accused belongs to the Christian community; this is not a court finding
Accused domicile/state: Not stated (complaint lists the news channel's address in Thiruvananthapuram)
Accused occupation: Editor, news reader and publisher of an online news channel; journalist (per appellant's submission)
Previous criminal record: No convictions stated. The complainant alleged he is a 'habitual offender' in creating controversies and failed to cooperate in another case (allegation only)
Victim socioeconomic status: Sitting MLA (Kunnathunad, SC-reserved constituency); President of District Sports Council
Accused–victim relationship: No personal relationship stated; Court observed the parties appear to be on inimical terms
Offence category: Alleged caste-based insult/humiliation; nuisance via communication (Court: at best defamation)
Statute: SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989; Kerala Police Act; (IPC s.500 noted by Court)
Statutory provision: SC/ST Act s.3(1)(r), s.3(1)(u); Kerala Police Act s.120(o)
Offence severity: SC/ST Act s.3(1)(r)/(u): 6 months to 5 years and fine; KP Act s.120(o): up to 1 year or fine up to Rs 5,000, or both
Physical harm: No physical harm; complainant alleged humiliation, mental pain and agony
Motive: Court: no indication the statements were made because of complainant's caste; intention may have been to malign or defame
Key evidence accepted: Transcript of the YouTube video read together with the complaint
Post-offence conduct: Complainant alleged the appellant ignored notices to appear for interrogation (allegation, not a finding)
Bail history: Anticipatory bail refused by Special Judge (16-06-2023); HC dismissed appeal (30-06-2023); SC granted anticipatory bail
Legal representation: Senior counsel Sidharth Luthra and Gaurav Agrawal for appellant (whether private or legal aid not stated)
Investigation status: Investigation pending; State submitted a quashing petition was pending before the Kerala HC
Procedural irregularity: Courts below did not examine whether the insult was on account of the complainant's caste
Appeal history: Special Judge: anticipatory bail refused. HC: appeal dismissed. SC: appeal allowed
Prosecution argument: Complainant is an SC MLA from a reserved seat; video published knowing his caste, to humiliate him; caste name need not be mentioned; s.18 bars anticipatory bail; appellant non-cooperative
Defence argument: No reference to caste in video; journalist publishing researched facts; at most defamation; s.3(1)(u) requires enmity against SC/ST as a group; s.18 bar inapplicable without a prima facie case
Legal principle applied: s.18 bar on anticipatory bail applies only where a prima facie offence under the Act is made out; s.3(1)(r) requires insult because of caste identity, and mere knowledge of caste is insufficient; s.3(1)(u) concerns the group, not individuals; strict construction of penal statutes
Precedent relied upon: Prathvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India (2020) 4 SCC 727; Hitesh Verma v. State of Uttarakhand (2020) 10 SCC 710; Ramesh Chandra Vaishya v. State of UP 2023 SCC OnLine SC 668; State of MP v. Ram Krishna Balothia (1995) 3 SCC 221; Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra (2018) 6 SCC 454; Vilas Pandurang Pawar v. State of Maharashtra (2012) 8 SCC 795; Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre v. State of Maharashtra (2011) 1 SCC 694; Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) 8 SCC 273; Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022) 10 SCC 51; Rahna Jalal v. State of Kerala (2021) 1 SCC 733
Other sentence/order: If arrested in FIR No. 899/2023 (Elamakkara PS), to be released on bail on conditions set by the Investigating Officer; complainant free to prosecute for defamation

Case ID: Mohd. Firoz v. State of Madhya Pradesh; Crl. Appeal No. 612 of 2019
Court / Bench: Supreme Court of India; Uday Umesh Lalit J, S. Ravindra Bhat J, Bela M. Trivedi J (author)
Case type: Criminal appeal against conviction and death sentence
Original court: High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur (judgment 15-07-2014; Crl. Ref. 09/2013, Crl. Appeals 2920/2013 & 3132/2013); trial by Sessions Court, Seoni
Number of accused: 2 at trial (A2 acquitted by HC; acquittal final)
Accused domicile/state: Native place in Bihar (arrested at Husainabad, PS Mojahidpur, Bhagalpur); told victim's family he had come from Gorakhpur; working in Madhya Pradesh
Accused disability/health: Not stated (SC called for psychiatric and psychological evaluation reports; contents not described)
Accused role: A1 principal offender; A2 charged as abettor (acquitted)
Accused–victim relationship: Stranger: came to the house that day with A2, who asked for a night's accommodation for him
Offence category: Kidnapping, abduction, rape of a child, and murder
Statutory provision: IPC s.363, 366, 376(2)(i), 376(2)(m), 302 (SC held s.376A also applicable); POCSO s.5(i) r/w 6, s.5(m) r/w 6
Weapon involvement: None; death caused by smothering of nose and mouth
Physical harm: Death (bronchopneumonia and cerebral hypoxia caused by smothering); genital injuries; multiple abrasions; lip lacerations
Number of offences: 7 heads of conviction affirmed, plus s.376A applied by SC
Premeditation/planning: Not expressly found; accused gave the victim's cousin bananas, sent him home, and took the victim with him
Evidence type: Circumstantial: last-seen witnesses, fruit seller, medical and post-mortem evidence, DNA, test identification parade, absconding, admissions under s.313
Key evidence accepted: Last seen together (PW1, PW6, PW7, PW31, fruit seller PW4); DNA match of hair found at the scene; about 12-hour gap before victim found; absconding to Bihar; medical evidence
Confession/admission: In s.313 CrPC statement, admitted visiting the victim's house with A2 and his arrest and transit remand; no confession
Witness credibility: Accepted. Defence attacked relatives as interested witnesses; rejected. Testimony of a ~4-year-old witness found truthful
Aggravating circumstances: Victim aged about 4; barbaric nature of acts; death caused by injuries inflicted during rape
Mitigating circumstances: Defence relied on family affidavits, jail documents and social inquiry report; SC called for probation, jail-conduct and psychological reports
Post-offence conduct: Absconded to native place in Bihar; offered no explanation for parting company with the victim
Custody duration: Arrested 23-04-2013; continuous custody to SC judgment not expressly stated
Trial duration: Incident 17-04-2013; Sessions conviction 2013 (exact date not stated); HC 15-07-2014; SC 19-04-2022
Legal representation: Legal aid throughout: trial court appointed a State-paid legal-services advocate for both accused as no advocate was ready to appear; in SC, Senior Advocate B.H. Marlapalle appointed through Supreme Court Legal Services Committee
Procedural irregularity: Defence alleged unfair trial (media pressure, common legal-aid lawyer, inadequate s.313 questioning); rejected as unsubstantiated and raised for the first time. s.376A not charged; SC held the omission immaterial under s.215 CrPC
Appeal history: Sessions: A1 death sentence (s.302) plus other sentences; A2 convicted. HC: A1's death sentence confirmed; A2 acquitted. SC: conviction affirmed; death commuted
Prosecution argument: Heinous crime; concurrent findings; admissions relieved half the prosecution's burden; last-seen proved; minor discrepancies immaterial; fair-trial plea raised first time in SC
Defence argument: Interested witnesses; incomplete circumstantial chain; last seen not proved; defective s.313 questioning; media pressure and unfair trial; not 'rarest of rare'
Legal principle applied: Five principles for circumstantial evidence (Sharad Birdhichand Sarda); last seen together with s.106 Evidence Act; inculpatory part of s.313 statement usable; 'rarest of rare' doctrine (Bachan Singh); restorative justice
Precedent relied upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116; Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684; Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (1983) 3 SCC 470; Shatrughna Baban Meshram v. State of Maharashtra (2021) 1 SCC 596; Mohan Singh v. Prem Singh (2002) 10 SCC 236; Rajender v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2019) 10 SCC 623; Satpal v. State of Haryana (2018) 6 SCC 610; Maneka Gandhi v. UOI (1978) 1 SCC 248
Sentencing rationale: Followed Shatrughna Baban Meshram (similar facts) to commute death to life for s.302. For s.376A, said imprisonment for remainder of natural life would have been appropriate, but imposed 20 years on restorative-justice grounds
Judicial mitigating factors: Restorative justice and opportunity for the offender to reform; line of SC precedent not treating similar cases as 'rarest of rare'
Judicial aggravating factors: Barbaric nature of the crime; victim's tender age; death of victim
Imprisonment type: Life imprisonment (s.302, s.376(2), POCSO counts); 20 years (s.376A); RI 7 years (s.363); RI 10 years (s.366)
Fine: Rs 2,000 for each of s.363, s.366 and s.376(2)/POCSO counts (trial court; affirmed)
Other sentence/order: All sentences to run concurrently; death sentence commuted
